newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to end peacekeeping in Angola; observers stay.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to end peacekeeping in Angola; observers stay.

text.p: With tensions rising in Angola, the U.N. Security Council voted unanimously on Monday to close its current peacekeeping operation and create an observer mission of 86 lighty-armed military officers and 345 civilian police.

The new operation, to be known as the U.N. Observer Mission in Angola or by its Portuguese acronym MONUA, officially takes over on July 1 from the U.N. Angola Verification Mission, called UNAVEM III, set up early in 1995.

The 4,000 U.N. troops attached to the current mission will withdraw slowly with two reduced infantry battalions staying until sometime in September. Another infantry company would stay to guard U.N. property until November.
The United Nations helped to implement the agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994 that ended nearly two decades of civil war in the former Portuguese colony.
"After a long and difficult path, the Lusaka protocol has finally entered its final stage," Angola's U.N. ambassador Afonso van Dunem Mbinda told the council.
"Although much still remains to be done, its positive effects are now so clearly apparent that we feel confident about the future," he said.

Over the past month, however, the Angolan government has been moving into diamond-rich areas held by the UNITA former rebels in the northeast. The Angolan government was emboldened to move against UNITA since Congo rebel leader Laurent Kabila took over in the former Zaire.

The war in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo, saw the participation of Angolan government troops on the side of the rebels and UNITA on the side of the former government of Mobutu Sese Seko, despite their respective denials.
The council's resolution did not specifically refer to this conflict, although U.S., British and French envoys mentioned it in their speeches.

Instead, the document said both the government and UNITA had to complete their obligations under the 1994 peace accords. The document pointed a finger at UNITA for not having demobilized all its troops, for broadcasting anti-government propaganda and for not permitting government administers into vast areas it controls.
"This is an important moment for Angola," said British envoy Stephen Gomersall, adding, however, that the momentum had slowed down in achieving reconciliation.
"In recent weeks military clashes have jeopardised the peace process" because of a buildup of military forces in the north, he said. "Tensions clearly remain high."

U.S. envoy Cameron Hume also expressed concern about "troop movements and ceasefire violations in the northeast provinces and called on the government to "desist immediately from unilateral military actions."

Angola's van Dunem Mbinda said the government took action in the northeast because of a "massive influx of people" coming from the former Zaire, including former Mobutu loyalists. He contended that 2,000 UNITA fighters were in Point-Noire in the Republic of Congo.
Specifically, the new mission will have 86 military observers, 345 civilian police, about 50 human rights monitors, and assorted civilian personnel.
Currently, the United Nations has about 5,000 personnel in Angola, including troops, military observers and civilian police from more than 30 countries.
